title: Parts of Speech — Deeper Dive
description: Go deeper into parts of speech for Grade 7: adjective order, pronoun-antecedent agreement, verb patterns (gerund vs infinitive) and extended collective nouns — with practice and tests.

topics.title: Adjective Order & Extended Collective Nouns
topics.concept:
When two or more adjectives describe the same noun, English follows a fairly fixed order: opinion, then size, then age/shape, then colour, then origin, then material.

  • a nice big old house (opinion–size–age)
  • a small square blue tile (size–shape–colour)

We usually do not put a comma between adjectives of different types (a big red ball), but we do between adjectives of the same type (a kind, gentle teacher).

Collective nouns name a group as one. Beyond 'team' and 'class', learn these:

GroupCollective Noun
lionsa pride
wolvesa pack
shipsa fleet
singersa choir
flowersa bunch / bouquet

examples.problem: Order the adjectives: wooden / old / a / chair / lovely
examples.solution: a lovely old wooden chair — opinion (lovely) → age (old) → material (wooden).

examples.problem: Collective noun for a group of lions?

recap: Order: opinion → size → age/shape → colour → origin → material
No comma between adjectives of different types (a big red ball)
Learn collective nouns: a pride, a pack, a fleet, a choir

topics.title: Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement
topics.concept:
A pronoun must agree with its antecedent (the noun it replaces) in number and gender.

  • Singular antecedent → singular pronoun: Each boy must bring his book.
  • Plural antecedent → plural pronoun: The students brought their books.

Watch these traps:

  • Indefinite pronouns like everyone, each, nobody are singular: Everyone took his/her seat. (modern English often accepts 'their').
  • Collective nouns take a singular pronoun when acting as one unit: The team won its match.
  • Two singular nouns joined by 'and' → plural pronoun: Ravi and Sam lost their way.

examples.solution: his/her (or 'their' in modern usage) — 'every student' is singular.

examples.problem: Correct: The jury gave their verdict (acting as one).
examples.solution: The jury gave its verdict. — acting as one unit, the collective noun takes 'its'.

recap: A pronoun agrees with its antecedent in number and gender
Collective nouns acting as one take a singular pronoun (its)

topics.title: Verb Patterns — Gerund vs Infinitive
topics.concept:
Some verbs are followed by a gerund (-ing), others by an infinitive (to + verb).

Verb + gerund (-ing)Verb + infinitive (to)
enjoy, finish, avoidwant, hope, decide
mind, suggest, practiseagree, promise, learn
keep, consider, admitplan, refuse, expect
  • I enjoy swimming. (not 'to swim')
  • She wants to swim. (not 'swimming')

A few verbs (like, love, hate, begin, start) accept both with little change in meaning: I like reading / I like to read.

examples.solution: to go — 'decide' is followed by the infinitive.

questions.q: Correct order:
'I enjoy ___ early.'
'She wants ___ a doctor.'
Collective noun for a group of singers:
Pronoun: 'Each of the boys raised ___ hand.' (strict)
Correct order:
'They avoided ___ late.'
'He promised ___ on time.'
Pronoun: 'The team celebrated ___ victory.'
'We finished ___ the project.'
Collective noun for wolves:
'She decided ___ the truth.'
Spot the error: 'He suggested to meet at the library.'
questions.explanation: 'suggest' is followed by a gerund or 'that' clause: 'suggested meeting'.

questions.q: Choose the correct order: 'She wore a ___ scarf.'
Identify the agreement error: 'Everybody should mind their own business.' (strict grammar)
questions.explanation: Strict grammar treats 'everybody' as singular → 'his or her'.

questions.q: Choose: 'I can't help ___ at his jokes.'
questions.explanation: 'can't help' is followed by a gerund.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: 'cattle' is a plural collective noun → 'are grazing'.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb pattern: 'She stopped ___ to greet us.'
options: to walk in order to greet
walking; she paused to greet us
Both B and C express it correctly
questions.explanation: 'stop + to-infinitive' means to pause in order to do something.

questions.q: Rearrange: 'old / charming / a / cottage / little / stone'
options: a charming little old stone cottage
a little charming stone old cottage
a stone old little charming cottage
an old stone little charming cottage
questions.explanation: Opinion → size → age → material: charming little old stone.

questions.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Neither Riya nor her sisters have finished ___ work.'
questions.explanation: With 'nor', agreement is with the nearer subject 'sisters' (plural) → 'their'.

outcomes: Arrange several adjectives in the correct natural order
Choose between a gerund and an infinitive after a verb
Use a wider range of collective nouns accurately

intro.en: You already know the eight parts of speech. This chapter sharpens the tricky parts: the order several adjectives must follow, making a pronoun match the noun it stands for, and deciding whether a verb is followed by -ing or to. These are the details that separate good English from great English.
intro.hi: आप आठ शब्द-भेद (parts of speech) पहले से जानते हैं। यह अध्याय कठिन भागों को निखारता है: कई विशेषणों का सही क्रम, सर्वनाम का अपनी संज्ञा से मेल, और यह तय करना कि क्रिया के बाद -ing आए या to। यही बारीकियाँ अच्छी अंग्रेज़ी को श्रेष्ठ बनाती हैं।

real_life.situation:
You describe a gift:

You: She gave me a lovely small round wooden box, and everyone said they loved theirs too. I can't wait to open it!
real_life.why: The adjectives fall in a fixed order (opinion–size–shape–material); 'theirs' agrees with the plural 'everyone'; and 'wait' is followed by the infinitive 'to open'. Each is a deeper parts-of-speech rule you'll master here.

rule_box.formula: Opinion → Size → Age/Shape → Colour → Origin → Material → Noun
rule_box.example: a beautiful little old brown leather bag

words.meaning: the noun a pronoun refers to
the -ing form used as a noun

quick_test.q: Which verb is normally followed by a gerund?
quick_test.explanation: 'enjoy' takes the gerund: 'enjoy swimming', not 'enjoy to swim'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Everyone must bring their own pen. (strict grammar)
common_mistakes.right: Everyone must bring his or her own pen.
common_mistakes.note: 'Everyone' is singular; 'their' is accepted informally but 'his or her' is strictly correct.
